Your New Dog's First Vet Visit: What to Bring and Ask

Plan a new dog's first vet visit with a bring list, the questions that matter, a cost worksheet you fill with local quotes, and a first-week readiness test.

Published: 2026-10-18Sources checked: 2Educational planning guide

Book the first exam within the first week of bringing a dog home, bring any prior records and a fresh stool sample, and use the visit to set a vaccine and parasite schedule with your veterinarian.

Why this one visit anchors the whole first year

The first veterinary appointment is less about fixing a single problem and more about building a baseline you will measure against for years. NAPHIA's owner guide suggests scheduling it within the first week of bringing a pet home, gathering any medical information from the breeder, shelter, or previous caregiver, and bringing a fresh stool sample in a sealed container so the clinic can check for parasites (NAPHIA). That early appointment is also where the veterinarian records your dog's starting weight, listens to the heart and lungs, and notes anything to watch as your dog grows.

How often you return depends on age, and knowing the pattern early helps you budget realistically. The Merck Veterinary Manual pet-owner version notes that puppies are typically seen every three to four weeks until about four months old, adult dogs at least once a year for a full checkup, and senior dogs over seven to eight years twice a year or more, because older dogs are more likely to get sick and may need blood tests or x-rays to catch issues early (Merck Veterinary Manual). A puppy therefore means several visits in the first few months, while an adult adoption usually means one anchor exam and an annual rhythm after that. Deciding which stage your dog is in tells you how many appointments to plan and reserve for.

What to bring so the visit is not wasted

Walk in with the paperwork and samples that let the veterinarian make decisions on day one, rather than scheduling a second visit to gather what you could have brought:

  • Any records from the breeder, shelter, or prior owner, including deworming dates, vaccine dates, and microchip numbers.
  • A fresh stool sample in a sealed or double-bagged container for a fecal test, which the manual notes clinics use to find parasites.
  • A written list of questions and anything odd you have noticed, such as changes in appetite, energy, coughing, or itching.
  • The food your dog is currently eating, by brand and formula name, so any diet advice is specific.

Bring the dog on an empty-ish stomach if car sickness is a concern, and use a secure carrier or leash so a nervous dog cannot bolt in the parking lot. Keep all these documents in one folder from the start; our vet record folder guide shows how to organize it so you are not rebuilding your dog's history at every clinic or boarding intake down the road.

Questions worth asking your veterinarian

NAPHIA's checklist highlights practical questions new owners often forget in the moment: when to switch from puppy to adult food, which toys and teething options are safe, when structured exercise and training can begin, and what breed-specific risks to watch for (NAPHIA). Because the exam room moves quickly, writing these down beforehand is the difference between leaving with a plan and leaving with regrets. Add these to your list:

  • Which vaccines does my dog need based on where we live and our lifestyle?
  • What parasite prevention do you recommend, and should it run year-round?
  • When would you recommend spay or neuter for this particular dog?
  • What early dental care should I start at home, and how often?

The manual notes that core vaccines recommended by nearly all veterinarians protect against illnesses like distemper, parvovirus, and rabies, while others such as Lyme disease or Bordetella matter in certain areas depending on where you live and your dog's lifestyle. It also explains that dogs should be tested for heartworm every year and stay on year-round prevention, and that a yearly fecal test screens for intestinal parasites, some of which can affect people in the household (Merck Veterinary Manual). Asking about these at the first visit lets you plan the recurring cost rather than being surprised by it. For a repeatable schedule, see our vaccination visit planning guide.

A first-visit cost worksheet you fill with local quotes

Prices vary widely by region and clinic, so instead of guessing, call two local practices, ask for their fees line by line, and drop the numbers into this worksheet. Multiply where a formula is shown, then add a reserve line for the add-ons that commonly appear once the exam is underway.

Line itemFormula
Exam feequoted exam price x 1 visit
Initial vaccinesper-vaccine price x number recommended at this visit
Fecal test + dewormingfecal price + deworming price
Parasite prevention startmonthly product price x months until next visit
Microchip (if not done)quoted one-time price
Booster follow-upsestimated visit price x remaining puppy visits
Reserve10-20% of the subtotal for add-ons

The booster line matters most for puppies, since the manual describes visits every few weeks until about four months. For the full-year and multi-year picture, feed these numbers into our five-year ownership cost framework and the first-year cost traps guide, which show how a single exam sits inside the larger budget.

A realistic first-week test

Before the appointment, run this dry run to see whether your routine is genuinely ready or only ready on paper:

  1. Day 1: Book the exam and start a folder with the dog's origin, current diet, and any records you received.
  2. Day 2-3: Practice short, calm car rides with treats so the clinic trip is not the dog's very first ride.
  3. Day 4: Confirm the clinic's sample requirements and plan to collect a fresh stool sample the morning of the visit.
  4. Day 5: Attend the exam, ask your written questions, and write down the vaccine and recheck dates before you leave the room.
  5. Day 6-7: Book the follow-up booster visit, which the manual notes puppies need every few weeks until about four months old (Merck Veterinary Manual).

If any step felt rushed or fell apart, that is precisely the part of your routine to shore up before the next appointment. A repeatable structure helps far more than memory does; our routine care calendar turns these one-off tasks into a schedule you can reuse each year.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Delaying the visit. Waiting past the first week means missing early advice and possibly a needed booster during the narrow puppy window.
  • Skipping the stool sample. The fecal test catches parasites that can affect the dog and, per the manual, sometimes people in the household, especially children; skipping it means a return trip.
  • Not writing questions down. Owners routinely forget half their concerns in the exam room, then remember them in the car.
  • Treating one visit as the finish line. The manual describes boosters given throughout a dog's life, some yearly and some every few years, so the first exam starts a schedule rather than ending one (Merck Veterinary Manual).
  • Forgetting to record the next date. Leaving without the recheck on the calendar is how gaps in prevention happen.

Turning the visit into a system

A single good appointment is worth little if the records scatter afterward. NAPHIA advises following the vet's instructions for medications, feeding, and training, scheduling the next appointment for booster vaccines, and keeping records organized for future visits (NAPHIA). Treat the exam as the first entry in an ongoing system rather than a task you complete and forget.

Right after you get home, add the vaccine dates, the recheck date, any prescriptions, and the weight the clinic recorded to your folder. Note which food and parasite product the vet endorsed so a boarding facility or a future clinic can pick up the thread instantly. This habit compounds: by the second or third visit you will have a clear timeline, which makes it easier to spot changes in weight or behavior and to answer the questions a veterinarian asks. It also saves money, because you avoid the duplicate tests and lapsed prevention that come from lost paperwork.

What this guide cannot tell you

This is planning help, not medical advice. It cannot tell you exactly which vaccines your dog needs, the right spay or neuter timing, or a diagnosis for any symptom you are seeing. Those depend on your dog's age, breed, health history, and where you live, and only an in-person veterinarian who has examined your dog can decide them. Local pricing also varies a great deal from clinic to clinic, which is why the worksheet uses quotes you gather rather than figures we invent. Use this guide to walk in prepared and organized, then follow the specific plan your veterinarian sets and keep the dates they give you.

FAQ

How soon should I take a new dog to the vet?
NAPHIA's owner guide recommends scheduling the first appointment within the first week of bringing your pet home. Booking early lets the veterinarian set a vaccine and parasite schedule, check the fresh stool sample you bring, and flag any breed-specific concerns before small issues grow. If you notice worrying signs sooner, call the clinic right away instead of waiting for the scheduled appointment date.
What should I bring to the first appointment?
Bring any medical records from the breeder, shelter, or prior owner, a fresh stool sample in a sealed or double-bagged container, and the current food listed by brand and formula. Add a written list of questions and notes about appetite, energy, or anything unusual. Having these on hand lets the veterinarian make decisions on day one rather than guessing about your dog's history or scheduling another visit.
Will one visit cover all the vaccines?
Usually not. The Merck Veterinary Manual notes puppies need vaccines every few weeks until about four months old, and boosters continue throughout life, some yearly and some every few years. Adult dogs typically get a full checkup at least annually. Plan for follow-up visits, and ask your veterinarian to write down the next dates before you leave so nothing lapses between appointments.
